title: Veridian: Leakage-Safe Heterogeneous Stacking for Multi-City AQI Forecasting
abstract: This research investigates whether heterogeneous stacked ensembles improve next-step Air Quality Index (AQI) forecasting relative to standalone models under leakage-aware chronological evaluation. The study evaluates six Indian cities using historical AQI, pollutant, meteorological and calendar features. Two proposed stacks combine XGBoost and a Temporal Convolutional Network with either Bi-LSTM (SE-1) or Bi-GRU (SE-2), using Extra Trees as a meta-learner. On 1,770 held-out observations, standalone XGBoost achieves the lowest overall RMSE (28.10), ahead of Extra Trees (28.37), SE-1 (30.81) and SE-2 (42.53). Ablation, city-wise, extreme-event, moving-block-bootstrap and SHAP analyses examine why increasing model complexity did not improve aggregate accuracy. The manuscript is in progress and has not been presented as a published paper.
content:
## Research question and scope

Does combining tree-based, recurrent and temporal-convolutional learners through heterogeneous stacking improve city-level Air Quality Index (AQI) point forecasts over competitive standalone models when the evaluation preserves temporal order?

The research covers **Delhi, Gurugram, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad and Patna**. It evaluates forecasting algorithms; it does not estimate the causal effect of particular emission sources or interventions. This is an **unpublished manuscript summary**, not an accepted conference or journal publication.

## Dataset and chronological evaluation

The manuscript reports **7,843 usable observations** after its preprocessing and historical-window requirements:

| Partition | Observations | Usable dates reported in manuscript |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Training | 5,203 | 22 Jan 2015 – 28 Feb 2019 |
| Validation | 870 | 8 Mar 2019 – 31 Aug 2019 |
| Held-out test | 1,770 | 8 Sep 2019 – 1 Jul 2020 |

Dates reflect the usable records, rather than implying every calendar day in those intervals is represented. City-wise missing-data handling and chronology-aware feature construction are described in the manuscript. Scaling parameters are fitted on training data, then applied to later partitions. Test data are kept separate from training, early stopping and model selection. Time-respecting out-of-fold predictions supply the stacking meta-learners, rather than in-sample base-learner predictions.

The tabular models receive **65 engineered features**, including historical AQI, pollutant and meteorological measurements, lagged values, shifted rolling statistics, calendar variables and city indicators. Sequence models process **14-step windows with 10 channels**. These are distinct representations, so reported differences should not be attributed solely to architecture.

## Models and stacking design

- **XGBoost:** standalone tree-boosting baseline.
- **Extra Trees:** standalone randomized-tree baseline.
- **Bi-LSTM, Bi-GRU and TCN:** sequence-learning baselines.
- **SE-1:** XGBoost + Bi-LSTM + TCN, combined using an Extra Trees meta-learner.
- **SE-2:** XGBoost + Bi-GRU + TCN, combined using an Extra Trees meta-learner.

The two stacks preserve the XGBoost, TCN and Extra Trees meta-learning components while changing the recurrent learner. Their comparisons test whether heterogeneous prediction signals are sufficiently complementary to improve point accuracy; complexity alone is not assumed to be beneficial.

## Held-out forecasting performance

The following are the manuscript's overall results on the same **1,770-observation held-out test set**. Lower RMSE, MAE and MAPE are better; higher R² is better.

| Model | RMSE | MAE | MAPE (%) | R² |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **XGBoost** | **28.10** | **18.51** | **14.02** | **0.9225** |
| Extra Trees | 28.37 | 18.63 | 14.26 | 0.9210 |
| SE-1 | 30.81 | 21.79 | 17.92 | 0.9068 |
| SE-2 | 42.53 | 34.60 | 32.62 | 0.8224 |
| TCN | 45.55 | 29.01 | 17.21 | 0.7963 |
| Bi-GRU | 108.15 | 68.47 | 42.74 | -0.1482 |
| Bi-LSTM | 109.69 | 68.55 | 41.17 | -0.1810 |

**Main finding:** XGBoost achieves the strongest overall point-forecasting performance. Neither heterogeneous stack surpasses either leading tree-based baseline on aggregate RMSE. These findings apply to the evaluated configurations and data; they do not establish that recurrent or convolutional models are inherently inferior for AQI forecasting.

## Ablation and component contribution

Removing XGBoost from the fitted stacks increases RMSE to **61.93 for SE-1** and **88.40 for SE-2**, identifying its large contribution to the fitted ensembles. Removing TCN instead reduces RMSE to **29.84 from 30.81** in SE-1, and to **38.32 from 42.53** in SE-2. These are results for particular fitted ablation configurations and do not prove causality or a universal ranking of model families.

## City-wise, extreme-event and statistical analysis

Aggregate metrics obscure geographic variation. In the manuscript, XGBoost has the lowest RMSE in five cities, while **Extra Trees is better in Patna (31.63 versus XGBoost's 37.21)**. Performance across the held-out test period therefore should not be generalized as a uniform city-level advantage.

The manuscript separately examines **202 observations with AQI greater than 300**, finding substantial underprediction during severe episodes. On this extreme subset, the small numerical RMSE advantage of SE-2 over XGBoost does **not** have statistical support under the reported adjusted bootstrap comparison. Selection of the subset by observed AQI and its discontinuous high-pollution clusters complicate interpretation.

For the full held-out test period, the manuscript reports a **paired, city-stratified moving-block bootstrap** using **10,000 resamples**, a primary block length of **seven days**, and fixed seed **42**. Under the stated resampling assumptions, comparisons support higher aggregate errors for both fitted stacks than the strong tree-based baselines. These intervals describe variation from resampling fixed-model test predictions; they do **not** measure uncertainty from retraining models under different random initializations or data samples.

## Explainability findings

Feature-level SHAP attribution for XGBoost emphasizes the previous day's PM2.5 concentration and AQI, with reported mean absolute SHAP contributions of **54.50** and **20.32 AQI points**, respectively. Meta-level SHAP allocates **80.61%** of normalized attribution to XGBoost in SE-1 and **78.26%** in SE-2. These describe behavior of the fitted models, **not causal effects of pollutants or proof that each learner improves forecasting accuracy**.

## Limitations and research integrity

1. The evaluation uses six cities and **one chronological held-out period** (September 2019 to July 2020); generalization to other locations or time periods is not established.
2. The test period overlaps **COVID-19 lockdowns in India**, representing an unusual distributional shift that was not separately isolated in the reported experiments.
3. Model configurations are fixed; systematic tuning and repeated independent training runs are not reported. Poor performance of a particular recurrent configuration cannot be generalized to every possible configuration.
4. Forecast reliability depends on the completeness, precision and temporal consistency of historical measurements; there are missing dates in the Patna test series.
5. Very high AQI observations can be underestimated. Evaluation specifically focused on extreme events and calibrated predictive uncertainty would be useful future work.
6. SHAP attributions are descriptive rather than causal. Statistical uncertainty estimates from fixed predictions do not cover training variability.

## Relationship to the research portfolio

**ECOSIMULATE** investigates assumed outcomes of hypothetical pollution-mitigation scenarios; **Veridian** investigates future AQI prediction under temporal evaluation; the proposed **AeroCausal** research would investigate causal attribution of upwind fire activity under explicit identification assumptions. These tasks require different evidence and should not be conflated.

*Publication record status: Publication in progress. The archive does not assert an accepted venue, DOI, publication date, verified manuscript byline or permission to distribute the manuscript PDF.*
